title: Null-conditional assignment, nameof and partial members
body: C# 14 allows `?.` and `?[]` on the left of assignments: `customer?.Order = GetOrder();` assigns only when `customer` is not null, and the right-hand side is not evaluated at all when it is null. Compound assignments such as `counter?.Value += 1` work too; `++` and `--` do not (CS1059). Using `?.` on an expression also tells nullable analysis that it might be null, so a later plain dereference of the same expression warns.

`nameof` now accepts unbound generic types: `nameof(List<>)` is `"List"` and `nameof(Dictionary<,>)` is `"Dictionary"`. Previously you had to write a closed type such as `List<int>` purely to satisfy the compiler.

Partial members let one part of a type declare a member and another part implement it, which is how source generators fill in code. C# 13 added partial properties and indexers; C# 14 adds partial instance constructors and partial events. Each needs exactly one defining declaration and one implementing declaration; only the implementing constructor may have a `this()`/`base()` initializer, and the implementing event must declare `add` and `remove`.

Other C# 14 refinements covered elsewhere in this guide: the `field` keyword (stage 3), implicit span conversions (stage 10), modifiers on simple lambda parameters (stage 8) and user-defined compound assignment (stage 3). File-based apps gained `#:package`, `#:sdk` and `#:property` directives so a single `.cs` file can reference NuGet packages.
When adopting `?.=`, check that skipping the right-hand side is intended: side effects there (logging, increments) no longer happen when the target is null.

challenge: Given a Node class with a Node? Next and an int Visits property, use null-conditional assignment to increment head.Next?.Visits by 1 for a two-node list and a one-node list, printing the visits of the second node when it exists.
question: In `customer?.Order = Compute();`, when is Compute() called?
correct: Only when customer is not null
wrong: Never; the statement is a compile error
reasoning: Null-conditional assignment evaluates the right side only after the receiver passes the null check.
